title: The biconcave red blood corpuscle is not a surface-tension equilibrium figure

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The biconcave red blood corpuscle is not a surface-tension equilibrium figure

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The biconcave mammalian red blood corpuscle is not a surface of constant mean curvature and so cannot be a fluid drop in equilibrium under surface tension alone; some other force, possibly osmotic inequilibrium or fluid-crystal forces of its cholesterin-like constituents, must maintain its shape, which changes to a sphere in diluted blood.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: biconcave corpuscle: 1/r_1 + 1/r_2 \neq \text{const}, so not a fluid drop in equilibrium under surface tension alone

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Accordingly, from the point of view of surface tension alone, the blood-corpuscle is not a surface of equilibrium; or in other words, it is not a fluid drop suspended in another liquid.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter V, “The Forms of Cells”; topic “Red blood corpuscles”. Scope: mammalian and other vertebrate red blood cells

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: biconcave corpuscle: 1/r_1 + 1/r_2 \neq \text{const}, so not a fluid drop in equilibrium under surface tension alone

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch05-24: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.86

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Surface geometry and osmotic shape changes map directly to standard measurements, and equilibrium models yield a decisive comparison. Existing public images are adequate to reject or support the surface-tension-only component, though they do not necessarily identify the exact alternative force.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reconstruct red-cell surfaces, compute mean curvature, and compare observed biconcave and osmotically swollen shapes with equilibrium surface-tension-only models and membrane-mechanics models.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Imaging preparation can distort curvature.

The suggested cholesterin mechanism is less directly testable than rejection of surface tension alone.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Biconcave geometry maps directly onto surface curvature, and a large open set of three-dimensional red-cell reconstructions contains the shapes required. A small team can test constant versus varying mean curvature with standard surface analysis. The hedged suggestion of osmotic or fluid-crystal forces is broader than the curvature test, but the negative claim that the corpuscle is not a surface-tension equilibrium figure is decidable now.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compute mean curvature over reconstructed mammalian red-cell surfaces and compare discocytes with cells that have rounded in hypotonic or spherocytogenic conditions. Constant mean curvature on the biconcave disc would refute the claim; curvature that varies over the disc, together with a shift toward a sphere when the medium is diluted, would support it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Its spherocytes are not a controlled dilution series, so the hypotonic-sphering clause needs a separate public experiment.

The library is human-dominated, so non-mammalian vertebrate corpuscles in the stated scope are thinly covered.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Measured red blood cells have a biconcave thickness profile whose upper surface has mean curvature of opposite sign at the central dimple and at the rim crest, so the cell surface is not of constant mean curvature (not a liquid-drop equilibrium figure), whereas rigid spheres imaged and analysed the same way show no such sign change.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py range-extracts 100 RBC and 50 bead ground-truth phase maps, subtracts each map's median, thresholds at 0.25 x the 99th percentile, labels 8-connected components, fills holes, and keeps objects not touching the border with aspect ratio <= 1.3 and footprint diameter >= 12 px. For each object it builds a 1-px radial profile about the centroid, takes r_crest at the profile maximum, fits t = a + b r^2 over pixels with r <= 0.3 r_crest (at least 4 pixels needed), and scores a centre-rim sign change when b > 0 and r_crest >= 0.25 r_edge. Fractions with a sign change in RBCs and beads are judged against the pre-registered thresholds. A sensitivity run with a 4 px bead diameter minimum (not pre-registered) is reported. Per-object rows are in derived/objects.csv, the summary in derived/summary.json.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Data: ground-truth quantitative phase maps of red blood cells (gt_phase1.mat ... gt_phase100.mat, red_blood_cell/train) and of 3 um polystyrene beads (gt_phase1.mat ... gt_phase50.mat, polystyrene_bead/train) from Figshare 21378744. Phase is proportional to optical thickness; the upper surface is taken as z = t/2 (cell symmetric about its mid-plane). Isolated objects are segmented by thresholding the background-subtracted phase, keeping connected components not touching the patch border, with aspect ratio <= 1.3 and footprint diameter >= 12 px. For each object the azimuthally averaged profile t(r) is computed about its centroid; r_crest = radius of maximum t; the centre curvature sign is the sign of b in a fit t(r) = a + b r^2 over r <= 0.3 r_crest. On the upper surface the mean curvature at the crest is negative (convex, since t'(r_crest) = 0 and t'' < 0) and at the centre it is positive (concave) when b > 0 and r_crest >= 0.25 r_edge; that sign change does not depend on the lateral or phase-to-height calibration. SUPPORTS if >= 70% of analysable RBCs show the sign change and <= 10% of analysable beads do.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. REFUTES if <= 30% of analysable RBCs show the sign change while <= 10% of beads do (RBCs are dome-like, consistent with a drop). MIXED if between 30% and 70%. INCONCLUSIVE (underpowered) if fewer than 30 analysable RBCs or 10 analysable beads; INCONCLUSIVE (other) if > 10% of beads show a sign change (the method manufactures dimples).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: fraction of analysable red cells whose upper-surface mean curvature changes sign between the central dimple and the rim crest

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: 1148 RBC profiles from 100 unique phase maps; pre-registered bead control: 41 analysable beads

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Thompson's argument is that a fluid drop held by surface tension alone must have constant mean curvature 1/r1 + 1/r2 everywhere, and the biconcave corpuscle does not. We test the geometric premise on measured cells: a closed surface whose upper face is concave at the centre and convex at the rim cannot have constant mean curvature. The thickness map from quantitative phase imaging is used with the standard mid-plane symmetry assumption. The second clause, that corpuscles become spherical in diluted blood, and the suggested osmotic or fluid-crystal causes are not tested here. Species of the donor blood is taken from the data source's description; scope is mammalian red cells.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: 3um polystyrene bead & red blood cell & histological slide datasets (Lee, Song, Kim, Ye, Jang), shared for the study 'Deep learning based on parameterized physical forward model for adaptive holographic imaging with unpaired data'

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The bead control failed: 38 of the 41 analysable bead objects (93%) show the same centre-rim sign change as the red cells, with a similar central dip (median 51% of the crest). Under the pre-registered rule this means the method manufactures dimples, so the 73% of red cells showing a sign change (1148 profiles; 70% was the pass mark) cannot be counted as support.

Why the control fails: single 3 um beads are only ~7.6 px across in these maps, too small to give the 4 central pixels the centre fit needs, so none of them is analysable. The beads that pass the 12 px size cut are 12-16 px objects with ring-shaped phase profiles, probably clusters or reconstruction artefacts rather than single spheres. The control therefore tests a different object class from the one intended, and a sphere control at red-cell scale (>= 12 px) would be needed. The 4 px sensitivity run changes nothing, because the extra beads are still too small for the centre fit.

The pre-registration listed bead files as gt_phase{1..50}.mat; in the archive they are named bead_gt_phase{1..50}.mat, which were used. It listed RBC files gt_phase{1..100}.mat; the archive numbers RBC files in blocks of 50 (1-50, 501-550, 1001-1050, ...), so the first 100 in numeric order (1-50 and 501-550) were used. Both are naming deviations, not changes of criteria.

Descriptively, most red cells do have a central thickness minimum and a rim maximum, as Thompson says. This test only fails to separate that from what the method finds in non-cell objects.

The dataset description does not state the donor species of the red cells; scope is assumed to be human or mammalian blood. Phase maps are network-training ground truths from one instrument; mid-plane symmetry (z = t/2) is assumed.

The sphering-in-diluted-blood clause and Thompson's suggested causes are not tested.

preregistered_at is the time of the pre-registration commit (0db9ed6a); the committed pre-registration carried an estimated time (21:40Z) written before committing. Data were first fetched after that commit (21:42Z); criteria are unchanged.
